## Overview

An agent decides for itself when to call a tool and with what arguments.
Its choices depend on everything it has read, including text an attacker
may have planted. So any tool you give it can end up being called in ways
you didn't plan for, and the tool itself has to enforce the limits.

This vignette shows securetools inside agents built with
[ellmer](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/). Each `tool_*()` function returns a
`securer::securer_tool()`. `securer::as_ellmer_tool()` starts a
`SecureSession` with those tools and gives the model a single tool that
runs R code in that session. The model's code can call the securetools
functions, and the limits (allowed folders, allowed tables, call caps) come
with each tool, so you don't write any checking code yourself.

The examples cover a single agent in a tool loop, a supervisor with
specialist workers, call limits, and custom tools next to the built-in
ones. For the tools themselves, see `vignette("securetools")`. For tool
calling in ellmer, see `vignette("tool-calling", package = "ellmer")`.

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(securetools)
library(securer)
library(ellmer)

# Set your LLM provider API key
Sys.setenv(ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "your-key-here")
```

## An agent with tools

ReAct (reason, then act) is the usual loop for an agent with tools. The
model reads the task, decides what to do, calls a tool, looks at the
result, and repeats until it has an answer. Every turn of the loop is
another tool call, and an agent that is confused or has been manipulated
can keep going for a long time.

ellmer runs this loop for you: `chat$chat()` keeps going until the model
answers without asking for another tool. With securetools, every call is
checked in the parent R process before the tool does anything. The model
can ask for whatever it likes; the tool only does what its limits allow.

Here is how one turn of the loop runs:

Register the tools with `as_ellmer_tool()`, so the model's code runs in a
securer session:

```{r react-basic}
# Create security-scoped tools
calc <- tool_calculator()
reader <- tool_read_file(allowed_dirs = "/path/to/project/data")

# A chat whose only tool runs R code in a SecureSession that has
# the calculator and the file reader
analyst <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = paste(
    "You are a data analyst.",
    "Write R code that calls calculator() and read_file() to answer questions."
  )
)
analyst$register_tool(as_ellmer_tool(tools = list(calc, reader)))

analyst$chat(
  "Read the file sales.csv from the data directory and calculate the total revenue."
)
```

`as_ellmer_tool()` starts a `SecureSession` (sandboxed by default) and
makes each `securer_tool` a function the model's code can call. The path
checks, the calculator's function list, and the call limits all run in the
parent process.

## A supervisor with specialist workers

Another option is to split the tools across several agents, so each one
has only what it needs. A supervisor agent reads the request and hands it
to the right worker. The supervisor has no securetools of its own.

Each worker gets its own `SecureSession`, with its own allowed folders,
allowed domains, and call limits. A file worker that gets hijacked still
can't make web requests, because it was never given that tool. The
supervisor only sees the workers' answers, not the raw tool output. You can
also set limits per role, for example a generous call limit for the data
worker and a tight one for the worker that writes files.

Each worker is its own chat. The supervisor reaches them through plain
ellmer tools that pass a question to a worker and return its answer:

```{r supervisor}
# Data worker: calculation and profiling
data_worker <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = paste(
    "You are a data specialist.",
    "Use the calculator for arithmetic and the profiler for data summaries."
  )
)
data_worker$register_tool(as_ellmer_tool(tools = list(
  tool_calculator(),
  tool_data_profile(max_rows = 50000)
)))

# File worker: reading and writing
file_worker <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = paste(
    "You are a file specialist.",
    "Read and write files as requested.",
    "Always specify format = 'auto' when reading."
  )
)
file_worker$register_tool(as_ellmer_tool(tools = list(
  tool_read_file(allowed_dirs = "/path/to/project/data"),
  tool_write_file(allowed_dirs = "/path/to/project/output")
)))

# One routing tool per worker
ask_worker <- function(worker, name, description) {
  tool(
    function(question) worker$chat(question, echo = "none"),
    description = description,
    arguments = list(
      question = type_string("The task for this worker, in full.")
    ),
    name = name
  )
}

supervisor <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = paste(
    "You coordinate a team.",
    "Send data questions to the data specialist",
    "and file operations to the file specialist."
  )
)
supervisor$register_tool(ask_worker(
  data_worker, "ask_data_specialist",
  "Ask the data specialist to do calculations or profile data."
))
supervisor$register_tool(ask_worker(
  file_worker, "ask_file_specialist",
  "Ask the file specialist to read or write files."
))

supervisor$chat("Read sales.csv, then calculate the mean of the revenue column.")
```

The workers keep their own chat history, so a later question to the same
worker can build on what it did before. Each `as_ellmer_tool()` call starts
its own session, which is what keeps the workers' tools apart.

## Call limits in agent loops

In an agent loop, the model decides how many times to call a tool. An agent
that misreads a task might call the calculator 500 times to "check" its
answer. A research agent might keep following links and hammer an API. Each
of those calls costs tokens and time.

securetools has two kinds of limit:

- `max_calls` caps the total number of calls to a tool. Once it's reached,
  every later call fails. This is the one that stops a runaway loop.
- `max_calls_per_minute` (only on `tool_fetch_url()`) caps how often the
  tool can be called. You might allow 1000 calls in total but only 10 a
  minute, so an external service isn't flooded.

When a limit is reached, the tool raises an error. securer passes the
error back to the model as the tool's result, so the agent can stop or,
for example, summarize what it already has instead of fetching more.

```{r rate-limiting}
# Cap the calculator at 50 calls for the life of the session
calc <- tool_calculator(max_calls = 50)

# URL fetch with both lifetime and per-minute limits
fetcher <- tool_fetch_url(
  allowed_domains = c("api.github.com"),
  max_calls = 100,
  max_calls_per_minute = 10
)

researcher <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = "You fetch data from APIs and analyze results."
)
researcher$register_tool(as_ellmer_tool(tools = list(calc, fetcher)))
```

The limits belong to the tool objects, not to the chat. If you give the
same `fetcher` to two sessions, they share its call count.

## Custom tools next to securetools

Most agents need something securetools doesn't have. You can put your own
`securer::securer_tool()` definitions in the same session as the built-in
ones.

```{r custom-tool}
# A custom tool alongside securetools
timestamp_tool <- securer_tool(
  name = "timestamp",
  description = "Return the current UTC timestamp.",
  fn = function() {
    format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)
  },
  args = list()
)

# Mix custom + securetools
assistant <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = "You help with data tasks and can check the current time."
)
assistant$register_tool(as_ellmer_tool(tools = list(
  tool_calculator(),
  tool_read_file(allowed_dirs = "/path/to/data"),
  timestamp_tool
)))

assistant$chat("What time is it? Also, what is 2^10?")
```

A custom tool's `fn` runs in the parent process, like the securetools
ones. The difference is that it only has the checks you write into it.
